newsitem.title: PERU: Negotiations begin in Peru hostage standoff.
newsitem.headline: Negotiations begin in Peru hostage standoff.

text.p: Negotiations were under way on Thursday in a standoff at the Japanese ambassador's residence between leftist guerrillas, threatening to kill hundreds of hostages, and representatives of the Peruvian government.

"The gentlemen of the MRTA (Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement) inform that a diligent mediation is being carried out in a reserved manner by representatives of the Red Cross," said Canada's ambassador to Peru, Anthony Vincent, one of five diplomats released by the rebels on Wednesday to act as their negotiating channel.
"The process is going to continue in the morning."

Vincent spoke to reporters after spending about 30 minutes back inside the compound apparently talking to the rebels at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima that MRTA guerrillas stormed in spectacular fashion on Tuesday night.
Vincent, who earlier held a two-hour meeting with Peru's mediator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo Cabrejos, did not give any more details of the negotiating process.

The rebels -- holding up to 484 people captive including high-ranking diplomats, businessmen and government officials -- demanded the release of 400 to 500 jailed comrades and the presence of President Alberto Fujimori for talks.
They said if the demands were not met they would kill the hostages.
Red Cross representative Michel Minning went into the compound around 7:30 a.m. EST (1230 GMT) for about 20 minutes. All inside were "fine, all calm," he said afterwards.
He said they immediately needed food and toiletries. "We will address the question of the negotiations later," he said.
Witnesses said three men, with shirt sleeves rolled up, were frequently looking out from behind a first-floor window, but it was unclear if they were rebels or hostages.
Fujimori, who ignored an ultimatum by the rebels for his presence on Wednesday, held his second emergency cabinet meeting since the crisis began in the early hours of Thursday.

Fujimori, in his second term as president, had won an apparent victory over leftist rebels who fought a 16-year war against the government by jailing the leadership of the Cuban- inspired MRTA and the better-known Maoist Shining Path.

But the MRTA showed it was far from dead with the daring Tuesday attack, assaulting the fortified compound from outside while apparently linking up with comrades disguised as waiters inside a cocktail reception.
Cartridges were smuggled into the residence beforehand among flowers and inside Christmas cake.

The rebels accidentally released Fujimori's mother and sister, but were still believed to be holding one of his brothers. The president, the son of Japanese immigrants, was believed due to attend the event but arrived late.

Guerrilla spokesmen said they attacked the Japanese ambassador's home to protest Tokyo's support for Fujimori and his economic policies. Japan was a target "due to the constant meddling of the Japanese government in Peru," the rebels said.
Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Iked was scheduled to arrive later on Thursday to help in the negotiations.

Outside the luxury residence in the middle-class district of San Isidro, family members, journalists and police continued an agonizing wait. The rebels said they had laid explosive booby-traps at the entrances of the residence to prevent police from storming the compound.

Estimates by the government and released hostages put the number of captives between 200 and 300. But a letter faxed from within the residence to family members of hostages and signed by captives said the rebels were holding 490 men. Six have been released since then.

Japan, Austria, Spain, South Korea, Panama, Malaysia, Venezuela, Bolivia, Brazil, Cuba, Guatemala and Honduras confirmed their ambassadors were among the hostages, while British and U.S. embassy officials were also present.
U.S. ambassador Dennis Jett attended the reception but left before the attack, according to the State Department.

Red Cross officials took supplies of food, water and an X- ray machine into the residence. Peru's largest human rights group said it had received a communication from the hostages warning the health of some was in danger.
But Peruvian cameraman Juan Victor Sumarriba, who was allowed into the residence, reported that the hostages were walking around and talking among themselves freely.

Governments around the world have urged Peru not to use force and to do everything it can to protect the hostages. The embassy home is legally Japanese territory, meaning Fujimori would theoretically need Tokyo's approval to mount an assault.
The captives also include Peru's foreign minister, agriculture minister, supreme court president, and the current and past chiefs of the anti-terrorism police.
The MRTA and Shining Path attempts to overthrow the government have cost 30,000 lives and $25 billion in infrastructure damage since 1980.
